answer.observations: Baseline r001 with defaults: udp_goodput_bps=979021120, udp_loss_frac=0.510489, tcp_goodput_bps=0, tcp_retrans=3, l1_util=0.999999, l1_drops=911591.

findings.text: tcp_goodput_bps=0 while UDP saturates l1 (l1_util=0.999999) and TCP retransmits only 3 segments.
findings.name: TCP starved by UDP

whys.result: With defaults, tcp_goodput_bps=0 while udp_goodput_bps=979021120 and l1_drops=911591.
whys.guess: The 2Gbps UDP flow keeps the sender-side FIFO queue full, so TCP packets are dropped before TCP can deliver payload.

whys.result: The default tcp_goodput_bps=0 occurs with l1.queue.length=100.
whys.guess: The 100-packet FIFO queue length is the proximate cause: a much shorter queue would reduce persistent fullness and allow some TCP packets through.

whys.result: The default tcp_goodput_bps=0 occurs with TcpCubic and tcp_retrans=3.
whys.guess: TcpCubic's loss-based response to UDP-induced drops makes TCP back off, while TcpBbr could maintain inflight and obtain bandwidth.

whys.result: The default tcp_goodput_bps=0 occurs with a FIFO queue on l1.
whys.guess: FIFO scheduling lets UDP monopolize the link; a scheduler queue that gives each flow an equal link share would raise tcp_goodput_bps.

hypotheses.text: Reducing l1.queue.length from 100 to 4 while keeping TcpCubic increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.
Changing tcp.type from TcpCubic to TcpBbr while keeping l1.queue.length=100 increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.
Replacing the sender-side FIFO queue on l1 with a scheduler queue while keeping default settings increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.

answer.observations: E1: q4 and bbr still have tcp_goodput_bps=0, while scheduler r004 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923. V3: the scheduler test was inconclusive because scheduler scheduling and queue-length effects were not separated.

whys.result: With scheduler queue r004 tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 while FIFO r001 is 0.
whys.guess: Per-flow scheduling gives TCP a service share, so TCP goodput is set by that share and packet overhead rather than by FIFO queue length or TCP variant.

whys.result: The scheduler run r004 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 with default queue length 100.
whys.guess: The scheduler result is caused by its 100-packet per-flow buffering; with l1.queue.length=4 the scheduler would starve TCP like FIFO.

hypotheses.text: At the same l1.queue.length (4 and 100) and TcpCubic, a sender-side scheduler queue gives higher tcp_goodput_bps than a FIFO queue.

answer.observations: E1 shows scheduler r004 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 while FIFO r001/r002 have 0; V3 says the scheduler test was not fair because queue-length and scheduling effects were not separated. F2 needs an explanation for r004 reverse utilization 0.009208 with no reverse drops.

whys.result: r004 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923, l1_util_back=0.009208, and l1_drops_back=0, while r001 has tcp_goodput_bps=0 and l1_util_back=0.0.
whys.guess: The reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic from the scheduler-given TCP flow; ACK volume is low enough that the receiver-side queue drops none.

whys.result: r001 has tcp_goodput_bps=0, tcp_retrans=3, l1_drops=911591, and l1_util=0.999999.
whys.guess: TCP is stalled in persistent RTO: FIFO tail drops its initial/probe segments, cwnd stays minimal, and exponential RTO limits it to a few retransmissions.

hypotheses.text: At l1.queue.length=100 and TcpCubic, a sender-side scheduler queue gives higher mean tcp_bps than a FIFO queue.
At l1.queue.length=4 and TcpCubic, a sender-side scheduler queue gives higher mean tcp_bps than a FIFO queue.

whys.guess: FIFO TCP is RTO-stalled: cwnd can open but only one segment stays unacked, so exponential RTO dominates and payload delivery is zero.

whys.result: scheduler r004 tcp_goodput=482007923 and r005 tcp_bps_mean=463881280, both near half of 1Gbps after overhead.
whys.guess: Scheduler gives TCP an equal service share; goodput is set by that share and packet overhead, not by TCP variant or larger queue.

whys.guess: Reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic, low enough that the receiver-side queue never fills.

answer.observations: E1/E2 show scheduler gives TCP about 482 Mbps at length 100 and 464 Mbps at length 4, while FIFO gives 0. T3-T12 show r001 TCP inflight stuck at 1448 bytes and RTO up to 8000 ms; T7/T8/T13/T14 show reverse device queue never fills.

E3/C5/V5: under sender-side scheduler at length 100, TcpCubic gives tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 while TcpBbr gives 190096915, so tcp.type matters. C6/V6: scheduler length 1000 gives 476482765, not above length 100.

whys.result: Under scheduler length 100, TcpCubic tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 while TcpBbr tcp_goodput_bps=190096915.
whys.guess: Under scheduler, tcp_goodput_bps is set by how fully the congestion control keeps its per-flow scheduler service share filled; loss-based Cubic-like variants fill it, while Bbr underfills it.

whys.guess: One of TcpBic, TcpLinuxReno, or TcpNewReno fills the scheduler share better than TcpCubic and gives more than 1% higher tcp_goodput_bps.

answer.observations: E4/C7/V7: under a sender-side scheduler at l1.queue.length=100, TcpCubic gives 482007923, TcpBic 482131872, TcpLinuxReno 482007923, and TcpNewReno 482007923, all within 1%, while TcpBbr gives 190096915. TcpVegas is still untested.

whys.result: Under scheduler length 100, loss-based variants are within 1% (482007923-482131872) while TcpBbr is 190096915.
whys.guess: TcpVegas's delay-based probing may avoid loss-induced backoff and fill the scheduler's per-flow share more steadily, giving more than 1% higher tcp_goodput_bps than TcpCubic.

hypotheses.text: With a sender-side scheduler at l1.queue.length=100, TcpVegas's tcp_goodput_bps is more than 1% above TcpCubic's.

experiment.question: Does TcpVegas fill the scheduler share better than TcpCubic?

answer.observations: E5/V8/C8: under scheduler length 100, TcpVegas gives tcp_goodput_bps=252144294, far below TcpCubic=482007923. E4/V7/C7: loss-based scheduler variants give 482007923-482131872 while tcp_retrans ranges 43-1901; F3 asks why retransmission count varies without changing goodput.

whys.result: TcpVegas under the scheduler measured tcp_goodput_bps=252144294 with tcp_retrans=0, while TcpCubic measured 482007923 with tcp_retrans=71.
whys.guess: TcpVegas, like TcpBbr, underfills the scheduler's per-flow service share because it backs off on delay/queueing rather than filling the share until loss.

whys.result: Scheduler runs at length 100 have tcp_retrans 43, 71, 92, and 1901 while tcp_goodput_bps stays 482007923-482131872 and UDP/drops are identical.
whys.guess: Under the scheduler, TCP's delivered goodput is set by its average service share; retransmissions are recoveries of TCP drops (l1_drops_tcp tracks tcp_retrans) and consume that same share, so variant-dependent retransmission counts do not change delivered goodput.

whys.result: TcpBic has tcp_retrans=1901 and TcpNewReno has tcp_retrans=43 while both deliver about 482 Mbps.
whys.guess: The retransmission spread reflects different average TCP inflight/service consumption by the variants, not merely different loss timing within the same service share.

whys.result: Changing tcp.type changes scheduler goodput, and length 100 gives 482007923 while length 4 gives 463881280.
whys.guess: l1.queue.length=200 could let TcpCubic fill the scheduler share more completely than length 100 and raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1%.

whys.result: TcpCubic already reaches 482007923 at scheduler length 100, and length 1000 gave 476482765, not a higher value.
whys.guess: At scheduler length 100 the service share is already filled, so length 200 will not raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1%.

With a sender-side scheduler at l1.queue.length=100, TcpBic and TcpNewReno have mean tcp_inflight within 10% of each other despite tcp_retrans=1901 and 43.

answer.observations: E6/C10/V10: under the scheduler at length 100, TcpBic has mean tcp_inflight 144380.08 and tcp_retrans 1901, while TcpNewReno has mean tcp_inflight 123075.656 and tcp_retrans 43, yet both deliver about 482 Mbps.

decisions.reason: The retransmission spread is explained by variant-specific inflight and loss behavior under the scheduler, while delivered goodput remains capped by the scheduler service share.

report.goal: Maximize tcp_goodput_bps, the brief's given goal.
report.limit: The scheduler caps TCP near half of l1 because UDP is locked and still offered 2 Gbps. Queue length 100 and 200 are equivalent; 1000 is slightly lower; TcpBic is 0.03% above TcpCubic, within tolerance, so not better. Other queue disciplines were not simulated, so the recommendation is the best among tested and mechanistically best because scheduler guarantees TCP a service share. Evidence: E1,E2,E3,E4,E5,E6,C5,C6,C7,C8,C9,V5,V6,V7,V8,V9.
report.explanation: With the default FIFO queue, UDP fills the sender queue and tail-drops TCP; TCP inflight stays at one segment and RTO stalls, so tcp_goodput_bps is 0. Replacing the sender-side FIFO with a per-flow scheduler gives TCP a round-robin service share, about half the 1 Gbps link after packet overhead. Loss-based TCP variants fill that share and deliver about 482 Mbps; Bbr and Vegas underfill it and deliver less. Queue length 100 is enough to keep the scheduler share filled; larger queues do not increase delivered goodput.

claims.text: Default FIFO gives tcp_goodput_bps=0 because UDP saturates the queue and TCP is RTO-stalled.
A sender-side scheduler queue raises tcp_goodput_bps from 0 to about 482 Mbps.
Under the scheduler, loss-based variants TcpCubic, TcpBic, TcpLinuxReno, and TcpNewReno give tcp_goodput_bps within 1% of each other.
Under the scheduler, TcpBbr and TcpVegas give lower tcp_goodput_bps than TcpCubic.
With the scheduler and TcpCubic, l1.queue.length=100 is at least as good as 4, 200, and 1000.
The large spread in tcp_retrans among loss-based scheduler runs reflects different inflight and loss behavior, not higher delivered goodput.
